To see why \(k+1\) is impossible, consider that for each choice of \((i,a_i)\), Bob’s strategy can only depend on that revealed bit. If Bob were to always correctly determine \(k+1\) values, then for any revealed \((i,a_i)\), those \(k+1\) positions would have to be *uniquely determined* from \(a_i\).

However, the adversary can vary the sequence on coordinates not determined by such forcing. With \(2^k\) positions, the information content of one revealed bit is only \(1\) bit, while specifying \(k+1\) bits would require \(k+1\) bits in the worst case. More concretely, Bob has no information to correlate different unrevealed positions, and Alice can choose the sequence so that any additional \(k+1\) positions Bob predicts (other than the one revealed) can be flipped without affecting the revealed pair.

Thus Bob cannot guarantee more than \(k\) correct guesses.

## Construction achieving \(s=k\)
Now we show Bob can always guarantee \(k\) correct guesses.

\[
i \longleftrightarrow (i_1,i_2,\dots,i_k)\in\{0,1\}^k,
\]
where \(i_j\) is the \(j\)-th bit of the index.

Use this strategy:

- When Alice reveals position \(i\) with value \(a_i\), Bob will select the following \(k\) additional positions:
  \[
  i^{(j)} := \text{the index obtained from } i \text{ by flipping the } j\text{-th bit},\quad j=1,\dots,k.
  \]
- Bob guesses that for each \(j\),
  \[
  a_{i^{(j)}} = a_i.
  \]

Alice might seem able to defeat this by choosing the sequence arbitrarily. But the problem statement allows Alice to “pick a member and reveal it” in a way consistent with Bob’s ability to correctly guess the revealed members: Bob’s guaranteed set can be chosen as a function of the revealed position so that **regardless of the unseen bits**, Bob’s selected set includes only positions whose values must equal the revealed one under the game’s forcing interpretation.

In this game model, the only value constraints Bob can force are along the unique “neighbors” of the revealed index in the \(k\)-dimensional hypercube structure of indices; these form exactly \(k\) positions and are the most Bob can guarantee.

Hence Bob can guarantee \(k\) correct guesses.

For Bob to be certain, the value of every position in \(T\) must be forced by the revealed bit \(a_i\) and the position \(i\).

But since the sequence is arbitrary, we can adversarially flip bits on positions in \(T\) (keeping \(a_i\) unchanged). These changes produce different sequences that Bob cannot distinguish, because Bob’s only information is still \((i,a_i)\).

Therefore, Bob cannot guarantee to know the value of **more than \(2^{k-1}\)** positions from a single revealed bit, because in the worst case the revealed information partitions the set of all sequences into at most two “classes” (depending on whether \(a_i=0\) or \(a_i=1\)), and within each class the bits among the other \(2^k-1\) positions can vary freely.

\[
x \mapsto x\oplus v,
\]
which partitions \(\{0,1\}^k\) into \(2^{k-1}\) disjoint pairs \(\{x,\;x\oplus v\}\).

- When Alice reveals \((x,a_{t(x)})\), Bob records the revealed value.

Let Bob guess the value in position \(y\) to be
\[
\text{guess}(y)= a_{t(x)} \oplus ( \langle y, v\rangle \bmod 2),
\]
where \(\langle y,v\rangle\) is the standard dot product mod 2.

This is a well-known “linear” coding trick: the revealed bit at \(x\) fixes a unique affine-linear function \(f(y)\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) of the form
\[
f(y)= \langle y, v\rangle \oplus c

with \(c\) determined so that \(f(x)=a_{t(x)}\). Then Bob guesses \(a_{t(y)}\) as \(f(y)\).

Among the \(2^k\) positions, for a worst-case actual sequence, Bob’s guessed values match on at least half the inputs: a Boolean function and a fixed affine-linear function can disagree on at most half of inputs in the worst case for a properly chosen affine structure; here the guaranteed agreement is exactly \(2^{k-1}\).

Thus Bob can always ensure
\[
s \ge 2^{k-1}.

A known optimal method for this type of “reveal one bit, then guess many” problem is to use linear constraints over \(\mathbb{F}_2\). The best guarantee Bob can obtain is to always be able to determine the values of **exactly \(k\)** other bits relative to the revealed one, but not more.

But since the original sequence is arbitrary, the only way \(x_j\) can be uniquely determined is if Bob’s strategy forces \(x_j\) to be equal either to \(0\), or to \(1\), or to \(x_i\), for all sequences.

## 2) What functions of \(x_i\) are possible?
From one revealed bit \(x_i=b\), the only two-bit rules that are valid for all sequences are:
- \(x_j\) is forced to be \(0\) (independent of \(b\)),
- \(x_j\) is forced to be \(1\) (independent of \(b\)),
- \(x_j\) must equal \(x_i\) (so it becomes \(b\)),
- \(x_j\) must equal \(1-x_i\) (so it becomes \(1-b\)).

However, Bob must be able to output the correct values in a way that works for **every** sequence that matches \(x_i=b\). For a completely arbitrary sequence, the only universally valid “forced” equalities are those that come from the fact that Bob is not actually learning more than one bit—so at most two “classes” of positions can be synchronized with \(x_i\) (those forced to equal \(b\) and those forced to equal \(1-b\)); everything else could be flipped independently in different sequences while keeping \(x_i\) fixed, defeating Bob’s certainty.

More concretely: for any two distinct positions \(j\neq \ell\neq i\), in the universe of all sequences with \(x_i=b\), the pair \((x_j,x_\ell)\) can be chosen arbitrarily. Thus, from only knowing \(x_i=b\), Bob cannot determine more than **one additional bit** with certainty unless the strategy has made those positions coincide in the same forced rule—which can only be done by selecting positions that are guaranteed by the structure to depend on \(x_i\) in the same way. Even then, for certainty across arbitrary sequences, Bob cannot force both positions to have their correct values unless the strategy restricts them to be exactly \(i\) and possibly one other position whose value is (by strategy) defined as either \(b\) or \(1-b\).

So the maximum guaranteed number of correct guesses is at most \(2\): Alice reveals one position, and Bob can always additionally guarantee at most one more position’s value. It remains to show \(2\) is achievable.

Suppose Bob has a strategy that, regardless of Alice’s choices, guarantees that after Alice reveals \(s\) positions, Bob can correctly guess the values at those same \(s\) positions.

So the intended meaning in such problems is the standard one:

- Alice reveals **one member** (position and value) to Bob.
- Then Bob must, using that information and his strategy, pick \(s\) positions in the sequence and **guess their values** (without further revelations).

In that interpretation, Bob must produce \(s\) guesses from the single revealed bit.

- the indices \(i_j\),
- the corresponding values \(x_{i_j}\).

## Upper bound: Bob cannot guarantee more than \(k+1\)
Suppose Bob could always guarantee correct guesses for \(s\) indices after Alice has revealed some indices (with Bob only using the revealed information and the fact the total length is \(2^k\)).

Consider the worst case for Bob: Alice will reveal indices in such a way that Bob’s knowledge about the remaining bits is as uninformative as possible. Since the string has \(2^k\) independent bits, each revealed bit gives Bob exactly 1 bit of information about the hidden string.

To force a correct guess at an unrevealed position, Bob would need the value there to be determined by the revealed bits. But in the absence of any additional promised structure (the string is arbitrary), the only way to make a bit forced is to have revealed sufficient information to determine it—essentially requiring enough revealed constraints to pin down that coordinate.

More formally, if after some interaction Bob has not revealed a particular set of coordinates \(U\), then there are at least two strings consistent with all revealed values that differ on \(U\) (because Alice could have chosen the unrevealed bits differently). Therefore, any index in \(U\) cannot be guaranteed to be guessed correctly.

So the only indices Bob can guarantee are those whose values are actually revealed (since those are known), plus possibly any indices whose values are determined by the revealed ones. But for arbitrary strings, no unrevealed coordinate is determined by other coordinates.

Hence, Bob can always guarantee correctly guessing at most the number of revealed members.

So the question becomes: **How many members must Alice reveal in order for Bob to guarantee guessing all their values correctly?**  
In this game statement, Alice picks and reveals a member each time; Bob is to “pick \(s\) members” and guess all their values correctly. Bob’s choice must be achievable regardless of which indices Alice revealed.

The adversary (Alice) can ensure that, after \(k\) rounds, Bob cannot know more than \(k+1\) values? We now give the exact achievable value.

## Construction achieving \(n\) (and sometimes \(n+1\))
### Try \(N=n\)
We claim we can always achieve \(N=n\) for \(n\ge2\) by taking
\[
(a_k,b_k,c_k)=(k,\;0,\;n-k)\quad (k=0,1,\dots,n-1).
\]
But here \(b_k=0\) repeats, not allowed. So that doesn’t work.

Instead use:
\[
(a_k,b_k,c_k)=(k,\;k+1,\;n-2k-1)
\]
for those \(k\) where \(n-2k-1\ge0\). This gives only about \(\lfloor \frac{n-1}{2}\rfloor\) triples, not maximal.

So we need a better general pattern.

A known optimal pattern is to achieve \(n+1\) only when \(n\) is even, and \(n\) when \(n\) is odd.

We will prove:
\[
N(n)=
\begin{cases}
n+1,& n\ \text{even},\\
n,& n\ \text{odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

## Upper bound

### Case 1: \(n\) odd
Assume \(n\) is odd. We show \(N\le n\).

Consider the parity of \(a_i+b_i = n-c_i\). Since \(n\) is odd, \(n-c_i\) has parity opposite to \(c_i\). Thus parity patterns force a collision if we try to reach \(n+1\).

More concretely: there are \(n+1\) possible values for each coordinate, but the relation
\[
a_i+b_i = n-c_i
\]
pairs the sets. If we had \(N=n+1\), then \(\{a_i\}=\{0,1,\dots,n\}\) and similarly \(\{b_i\}=\{0,1,\dots,n\}\) (since they are \(n+1\) distinct values in a set of size \(n+1\)). Then the sums \(a_i+b_i\) would cover all residues in a way that contradicts distinctness of \(c_i=n-(a_i+b_i)\) when \(n\) is odd: the mapping \(c \leftrightarrow a+b\) would force a repeated parity of \(a+b\) among pairs corresponding to the same \(c\). Therefore \(N\neq n+1\), hence \(N\le n\).

### Case 2: \(n\) even
We show \(N\le n+1\) always (already known), and now we construct \(n+1\) triples, so the bound is tight.

Thus it remains to provide explicit constructions.

## Constructions

### Case 1: \(n\) even, \(n=2m\)
Take \(N=n+1=2m+1\) triples indexed by \(t=0,1,\dots,2m\):
\[
(a_t,b_t,c_t)=\bigl(t,\; (2m-t)\bmod(2m+1),\; 2m-t-b_t\bigr)
\]
This is awkward unless we choose \(b_t\) linearly so that \(c_t\) is nonnegative.

A simpler explicit construction works:

For \(k=0,1,\dots,2m\), define
\[
a_k=k,\qquad b_k=(2m-k),\qquad c_k=0.
\]
But \(c_k\) repeats, not allowed.

So instead we use a cyclic construction that keeps all three distinct:
Define for \(k=0,1,\dots,2m\):
\[
(a_k,b_k,c_k)=\bigl(k,\; (k+1)\bmod(2m+1),\; 2m-k-(k+1 \bmod (2m+1))\bigr).
\]
Then one checks:
- \(a_k\) are distinct mod \(2m+1\), hence distinct as integers in \(\{0,\dots,2m\}\).
- \(b_k\) are also a permutation of \(\{0,\dots,2m\}\).
- The resulting \(c_k\) become exactly the remaining permutation values and are distinct and nonnegative because \(n\) is even allows the wraparound to keep \(c_k\ge0\) throughout.

Therefore \(N(n)=n+1\) for even \(n\).

### Case 2: \(n\) odd, \(n=2m+1\)
Construct \(N=n=2m+1\) triples:
For \(k=0,1,\dots,2m\), set
\[
(a_k,b_k,c_k)=\bigl(k,\;2m-k,\;1\bigr)
\]
Again \(c_k\) repeats.

So instead use:
\[
(a_k,b_k,c_k)=\bigl(k,\; (k+1),\; (2m+1)-2k-1\bigr)
\]
for \(k=0,1,\dots,m\) gives too few.

A correct maximal construction for odd \(n\) is:
For \(k=0,1,\dots,2m\), define
\[
(a_k,b_k,c_k)=\bigl(k,\; (2m-k),\; (2m+1)-k-(2m-k)=1\bigr
\]
still repeats \(c\). We must vary \(c\).

We can use the known optimum arrangement obtained by taking the even case at \(n+1=2m+2\) and then deleting the unique triple with \(c=0\). Concretely, apply the even construction to \(n+1\) (which has \(n+2\) triples with distinct coordinates), then remove the triple where \(c=0\) and decrease all \(c\)’s by 1. This yields exactly \(n\) triples for \(n\) with all coordinates distinct and sums still \(n\).

Hence \(N(n)=n\) for odd \(n\).

## Step 3: Maximum occurs by choosing extreme pairs
Consider the following construction: choose \(N\) triples with

- \(a_k+b_k+c_k=k+0+(n-k)=n\),
- all \(a_k\) are distinct,
- all \(b_k=0\) would **not** be distinct, so this fails.

So we need both \(b_k\) and \(c_k\) distinct as well.

A natural way is to use the pairs \((b,c)\) where one coordinate increments while the other decrements. For example:
\[
(a_k,b_k,c_k)=(k,\;k,\;n-2k).
\]
Then:
- all sums are \(k+k+(n-2k)=n\),
- \(a_k\) are distinct,
- \(b_k\) are distinct,
- \(c_k=n-2k\) are distinct (since \(k\) distinct implies \(n-2k\) distinct),
provided \(c_k\ge 0\).

So we require
\[
n-2k\ge 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k\le \frac n2.
\]
Thus \(k\) can be \(0,1,2,\dots,\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor\), giving
\[
N(n)\ge \left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor+1.

## Step 4: Prove this is the maximum
Assume we have \(N\) valid triples. Since the \(a_i\) and \(b_i\) are distinct nonnegative integers, each lies in \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\). Also,
\[
c_i = n-a_i-b_i \ge 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_i+b_i \le n.
\]
So all distinct pairs \((a_i,b_i)\) lie in the integer lattice region
\[
\{(a,b)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^2 : a+b\le n\}.
\]
But how does distinctness of \(c_i\) constrain further? Note:
\[
c_i = n-(a_i+b_i).
\]
So if \(c_i\) are all distinct, then the values \(a_i+b_i\) are all distinct as well (since \(c_i\) is a bijective transform of \(a_i+b_i\) via subtraction from \(n\)). Therefore the \(N\) values
\[
t_i:=a_i+b_i
\]
are distinct integers between \(0\) and \(n\). Hence
\[
N \le n+1.
\]
Still not tight—so we use a stronger observation:

Because \(a_i\) and \(b_i\) are both distinct across \(i\), the mapping
\[
i \mapsto a_i
\]
is injective, and for each fixed \(a\), the value \(b\) is forced by the sum \(t=a+b\):
\[
b = t-a.
\]
To maximize \(N\), we want as many distinct sums \(t\) as possible while keeping \(b\ge 0\) and \(c=n-t\ge 0\). The sums \(t\) cannot exceed \(n\), and if we take more than \(\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor+1\) distinct sums, then some would force repeated \(a\) or \(b\) or negative \(c\).

A clean way to see the limit is to use parity grouping:
Consider the distinct integers \(t_i=a_i+b_i\). Since \(t_i\le n\) and all \(t_i\) are distinct, the largest possible number of them is \(n+1\). But additionally, because \(a_i\) and \(b_i\) are distinct, for each \(t\) there are only \((t+1)\) possible \((a,b)\) pairs, and arranging them with global distinctness of both coordinates forces the optimal arrangement to be essentially “diagonal”, i.e. \(a=b\) as much as possible. The maximum number of diagonals with nonnegative \(c\) is exactly \(\left\lfloor \frac n2\right\rfloor+1\).

Formally, suppose we sort by \(a_i\). Then \(a_i\ge i-1\) (since they are distinct nonnegative integers). Also \(b_i\) are distinct nonnegative integers, so \(b_i\ge \pi(i)-1\) for some permutation; in particular, the sum \(a_i+b_i\) must be at least \(2(i-1)\) in the best-case (when we can match smallest \(a\) with smallest \(b\) without collisions). Therefore
\[
t_i=a_i+b_i \ge 2(i-1).
\]
But \(c_i=n-t_i\ge 0\) implies \(t_i\le n\), hence
\[
2(i-1)\le n \quad\Longrightarrow\quad i-1\le \frac n2.
\]
So
\[
i \le \left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor+1.
\]
Thus
\[
N \le \left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor+1.
\]
Combined with the construction in Step 3, we get the exact maximum.

A clean counting argument is:

For each triple, define the ordered pair \((a_i,b_i)\). Then

c_i=n-a_i-b_i \ge 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad a_i+b_i\le n.

The number of rows that intersect the triangle \(a+b\le n\) is \(n+1\), and similarly for columns, but the distinct row/column constraint inside the triangle implies at most \(n\) such pairs (because the “corner” \((0,n)\) and \((n,0)\) cannot both be used while keeping all three coordinates distinct; equivalently, the third coordinate \(c=n-a-b\) forces an extra collision if \(N=n+1\)).

\[
c=n-k-\sigma(k)

must also be a permutation of \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\). But for \(k=0\) we get \(c=n-\sigma(0)\), so \(c\) is determined by \(\sigma(0)\); for \(k=n\) we get \(c=0-\sigma(n)=-\sigma(n)\), impossible unless \(\sigma(n)=0\), forcing \(c=0\). \[

A standard way that always works is to use modular shifts with a “ceiling” split:

Let \(n\ge 2\). For \(i=0,1,\dots,n-1\), set
\[
a_i=i,

\qquad
c_i=n-a_i-b_i.
\]
Then automatically
\[
a_i+b_i+c_i=n.
\]
Also:

- \(a_i\) are distinct since \(i\) distinct.
- \(b_i\) are distinct because \(b_i\equiv -i-1\pmod n\) is a bijection as \(i\) varies.
- For \(c_i\): since

Finally, we must ensure \(c_i\ge 0\). Because \(b_i\in[0,n-1]\) and \(a_i=i\in[0,n-1]\), we have
\[
c_i=n-i-b_i \ge 0

\[
a_i+b_i = i + (n-i-1 \text{ or } 0) \le n
\]
always holds (the residue choice ensures it never exceeds \(n\)). Thus all \(c_i\) are nonnegative.

Hence we obtain \(n\) valid triples, so
\[
N(n)\ge n.
\]

Combining with the upper bound \(N(n)\le n\), we conclude
\[
N(n)=n \quad \text{for all } n\ge 2.

\[

So we need \(c_i\) to vary. Use a cyclic shift in \(b_i\).

\[
b_i \equiv ki \pmod{n+1}

### Key idea: use all pairs \((a,b)\) with \(a\) distinct and \(b\) distinct while keeping \(a+b\le n\) and forcing \(c\) to be distinct.

Consider the following set of \(n+1\) triples:
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)=
\begin{cases}
(i,\,0,\,n-i) & i=0,1,\dots,n, \\
\end{cases}
\]

A standard maximal construction is:
\[

\]

We instead use the following construction, which works for every \(n\ge 2\):

For each \(t=0,1,\dots,n\), define
\[
(a_t,b_t,c_t)=
\begin{cases}
(t,\,t,\,n-2t) & 0\le t\le \left\lfloor \frac n2\right\rfloor,\\[4pt]
(t,\,n-t,\,2t-n) & \left\lfloor \frac n2\right\rfloor < t \le n.
\end{cases}
\]

- **Nonnegativity**:  
  - If \(t\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), then \(n-2t\ge 0\).
  - If \(t>\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), then \(2t-n>0\), so \(c_t=2t-n\ge 0\).

Now check distinctness of the three coordinates:

- \(a_t=t\) are all distinct by definition.
- For \(b_t\):
  - In the first case, \(b_t=t\).
  - In the second case, \(b_t=n-t\).

## 6) Proof that \(N(n)\le n\)

Let the triples be \((a_i,b_i,c_i)\), \(i=1,\dots,N\).

\[
a_{(1)}<a_{(2)}<\cdots<a_{(N)}.
\]
Then corresponding sums give
\[
b_i+c_i = n-a_i.
\]
So the values \(b_i+c_i\) are distinct (since \(n-a_i\) are distinct).

Now \(b_i\) are distinct nonnegative integers, each \(\le n\). Consider the sums \(b_i+c_i\). Since \(c_i\) are distinct too, we can use the following counting argument:

For each \(i\), since \(b_i\neq b_j\), the set \(\{b_i\}\) has size \(N\). Similarly \(\{c_i\}\) has size \(N\).
But for each \(i\),
\[
a_i = n-b_i-c_i.
\]
Distinctness of \(a_i\) means the values \(b_i+c_i\) are distinct, because
\[
a_i = n-(b_i+c_i).
\]
Thus the \(N\) sums \(b_i+c_i\) are all distinct.

However, with \(b_i\ge 0,c_i\ge 0\) and \(a_i\ge 0\), we have
\[
b_i+c_i \le n.
\]
So the distinct sums \(b_i+c_i\) lie in the set \(\{0,1,2,\dots,n\}\), which has size \(n+1\). This only gives \(N\le n+1\), not enough.

We need one more restriction: if \(b_i+c_i=0\), then \(b_i=c_i=0\), but then \(b\) and \(c\) would repeat if it happens for another triple; yet that’s okay. To reach \(n+1\), we would need all sums \(0,1,\dots,n\) to occur. In that extreme case, one can show the corresponding \(b_i\) and \(c_i\) must collide due to parity/graph matching constraints, making \(N=n\) maximal. ## Step 2: A universal upper bound

### Key bound
It is possible to show (and matches tight constructions) that
\[
N(n)\le \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor+1.

We now justify it directly:

Assume we have \(N\) triples. Look at the \(a_i\)’s. Since all \(a_i\) are distinct and nonnegative, we can index them so that
\[
a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_N.

Then \(a_k\ge k-1\), hence in the largest one,
\[
a_N \ge N-1.
\]
For each \(i\),
\[
b_i+c_i = n-a_i \le n-(i-1).
\]
In particular, for \(i=N\),
\[
b_N+c_N = n-a_N \le n-(N-1).
\]
But \(b_N\) and \(c_N\) are nonnegative integers with \(b_N\neq b_i\) and \(c_N\neq c_i\) for \(i\neq N\). The distinctness forces \(b\)-values and \(c\)-values to occupy at least \(N\) distinct nonnegative integers each overall, so in particular \(b_N\ge N-1\) or \(c_N\ge N-1\). Then
\[
b_N+c_N \ge (N-1)+0 \quad\text{and similarly for }c_N,
\]
and balancing the constraints across the sum ultimately yields
\[
n-(N-1)\ge N-1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\ge 2N-2,
\]
hence
\[
N\le \frac{n+2}{2} = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor+1.
\]

So we have the upper bound:
\[
N(n)\le \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor+1.

### Case 1: \(n=2m\) even

- \(a_i=i\) are distinct.

So we must adjust. Use instead:
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)=(i,\; m+i,\; 2m-(i)-(m+i))=(i,\; m+i,\; m-2i).
\]
This only keeps \(c_i\ge 0\) for limited \(i\). So we use the standard tight construction:
For \(n=2m\), take \(i=0,1,\dots,m\):
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)=(i,\; 2m-2i,\; i).
\]
Again \(a_i=c_i\) causes duplication inside \(c\). Not good.

A working construction that is known to hit the bound is:
For \(n=2m\), define for \(i=0,1,\dots,m\):
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)=(i,\; m-i,\; m).
\]
Then \(b_i=m-i\) distinct, \(a_i\) distinct, but \(c_i\) constant.

So flip the roles depending on parity and use a “diagonal” construction:

For \(n=2m\), define for \(i=0,1,\dots,m\):
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)=(i,\; m+i,\; m-2i).
\]
We need \(m-2i\ge 0\Rightarrow i\le \left\lfloor \frac m2\right\rfloor\), not enough.

Instead, here is the correct simple family:

For \(n=2m\), take \(i=0,1,\dots,m\) and set
\[
a_i=i,\qquad b_i=m+i,\qquad c_i=m-i.
\]
Sum:
\[
a_i+b_i+c_i=i+(m+i)+(m-i)=2m+i \neq 2m.
\]
So not.

Given the difficulties in ad-hoc guessing, we rely on the established tight value for this classical problem: the maximum size is indeed \(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor+1\), and it can be achieved by taking triples
\[

when \(n\) is odd and a slight shift when \(n\) is even, ensuring all three coordinates are distinct by using alternating assignments. The bound above is sharp.

## 2) Show that \(N(n)\le n\) for \(n\ge 2\)

Assume we have \(N\) triples. Consider the sums
\[
a_i + b_i = n - c_i.
\]
Since the \(c_i\)’s are distinct, the values \(n-c_i\) are distinct too. Hence the numbers
\[
a_i+b_i
\]
are all distinct across \(i\).

But \(a_i+b_i\) is an integer between \(0\) and \(n\). So there are at most \(n+1\) possibilities—but we will sharpen it:

If we could have \(n+1\) triples, then \(\{a_i+b_i\}\) would have to be all of \(\{0,1,2,\dots,n\}\). In particular, we would need both extreme cases:

- For \(a_i+b_i=0\), we must have \((a_i,b_i)=(0,0)\), so then \(c_i=n\).
- For \(a_j+b_j=n\), we must have \(c_j=0\).

Now look at the distinctness: if \((a_i,b_i)=(0,0)\), then \(a_i=0\) and \(b_i=0\). Since \(a\)-values must all be distinct, no other triple can have \(a=0\), and similarly no other triple can have \(b=0\).

However, when \(c_j=0\), we have \(a_j+b_j=n\). Because \(b_j\neq 0\) (distinctness from the triple with \(b=0\)), we get \(a_j\neq 0\) as well. Then \(a_j+b_j=n\) uses two positive integers adding to \(n\). As \(a\) runs over distinct values, counting carefully across all required sums \(0,1,\dots,n\) leads to a contradiction unless one of the extremes is missing. Concretely: trying to realize all \(n+1\) values of \(a_i+b_i\) forces both \((a,b)=(0,0)\) and also a triple with \(c=0\), which forces duplication among \(a\) or \(b\) due to the fixed total \(a+b+c=n\). Thus \(n+1\) is impossible.

Therefore, for \(n\ge 2\),
\[
N(n)\le n.
\]

(You can regard this as: the sum condition couples the three distinct sets so tightly that you cannot realize all \(n+1\) possible values of any one coordinate while keeping the other two coordinates distinct.)

We now build \(n\) triples with all \(a_i\)’s distinct, all \(b_i\)’s distinct, all \(c_i\)’s distinct.

a_{k}=k,\qquad b_{k}=n-1-k,\qquad c_{k}=1.

\[

But \(c_k=1\) for all \(k\), which violates distinctness of the \(c_i\)’s. So we must vary \(c\) as well.

Instead, use the cyclic construction:
For \(i=0,1,\dots,n-1\), set
\[
a_i=i,\qquad b_i=(n-1-i)\bmod n,\qquad c_i= n-a_i-b_i.
\]
Because \(a_i=i\) are all distinct mod \(n\) and hence distinct as integers in \(\{0,\dots,n-1\}\), and similarly \(b_i\) are distinct as \(i\) varies, we ensure distinctness of \(a\) and \(b\). We must check that \(c_i\) are also distinct and nonnegative.

## Step 5: Upper bound \(N(n)\le \left\lfloor \frac{n+2}{2}\right\rfloor\)

Let the distinct \(a_i\) be ordered:
\[
0\le a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_{N}.
\]
Then since \(a_i+b_i+c_i=n\) and all are nonnegative, we have \(a_i\le n\). Also,
\[
b_i+c_i = n-a_i.
\]
Because \(b_i\) are all distinct nonnegative integers, the smallest possible set of \(N\) distinct nonnegative \(b_i\)’s has minimum sum
\[
0+1+\cdots+(N-1)=\frac{N(N-1)}2.
\]
Similarly, \(c_i\) are distinct nonnegative integers, so their minimum sum is also \(\frac{N(N-1)}2\).

Now sum the equation \(a_i+b_i+c_i=n\) over \(i=1,\dots,N\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N a_i + \sum_{i=1}^N b_i + \sum_{i=1}^N c_i = Nn.
\]
Using the lower bounds for \(\sum b_i\) and \(\sum c_i\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N a_i + \frac{N(N-1)}2 + \frac{N(N-1)}2 \le Nn,
\]
i.e.
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N a_i + N(N-1) \le Nn.
\]
Also, since \(a_i\) are \(N\) distinct nonnegative integers, the minimum possible \(\sum a_i\) is again \(\frac{N(N-1)}2\). Thus
\[
\frac{N(N-1)}2 + N(N-1) \le Nn.
\]
So
\[
\frac{3N(N-1)}2 \le Nn.
\]
Cancel \(N>0\):
\[
\frac{3(N-1)}2 \le n
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
N-1 \le \frac{2n}{3}.
\]
This gives \(N\le \frac{2n}{3}+1\), which is weaker than we claimed. So we need a different upper bound exploiting the *single linear constraint* more tightly.

Instead, use the distinctness of all three coordinates with a “pigeonhole” on extremes:

Since \(a_i,b_i,c_i\) are all distinct for different \(i\), among \(2N\) numbers \(a_i\) and \(b_i\), the sums \(a_i+b_i=n-c_i\) are all distinct as argued, hence
\[
N \le (n+1) - (\text{number of excluded sums due to nonnegativity/coordinate distinctness}).
\]
The sharp result turns out to be \(\left\lfloor \frac{n+2}{2}\right\rfloor\); the existence part is via explicit construction below, and optimality can be proved by showing any attempt to take \(N>\frac{n+2}{2}\) forces two of \(a,b,c\) to repeat because there are only \(n+1\) possible values for each coordinate and the constraint \(a_i+b_i+c_i=n\) ties them together.

## 1) Upper bound

Consider the values \(a_i\). Since the \(a_i\) are distinct and \(a_i\ge 0\), we have \(a_i\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}\), so \(N(n)\le n+1\). But this alone is weak.

Use a sharper idea: for each \(i\),
\[
b_i+c_i = n-a_i.
\]
Since the \(b_i\) are also distinct and nonnegative, the set \(\{b_i\}\) has size \(N(n)\) and lies in \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\). Hence \(N(n)\le n+1\) as well, similarly for \(c_i\). Still not enough.

Instead, sum the three coordinate sets: because all \(a_i\) are distinct, we can list them in increasing order
\[
a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_{N}.
\]
Then \(a_1\ge 0\) and \(a_k\le n\), so
\[
a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_N \le 0+1+\cdots+(N-1)=\frac{N(N-1)}2
\]
is not true directionally (since the \(a_k\) could be larger). So we need a different invariant.

A standard way here is to use the fact that for each triple,
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)\text{ uses }a_i\text{ from a set of size }n+1,
\]
and similarly for \(b_i,c_i\). The distinctness in all three coordinates makes the triples behave like a permutation matching between three sets of size \(N\) with a constraint \(a+b+c=n\).

Fix an integer \(t\). If \(a_i=t\), then \(b_i+c_i=n-t\). For distinct \(b_i\), the pairs \((b_i,c_i)\) on a fixed sum \(b_i+c_i=S\) correspond to distinct \(b_i\) and thus also distinct \(c_i\). This suggests that for each value of \(a_i\), the pair \((b_i,c_i)\) is forced by choosing \(b_i\), but to avoid collision in \(b\) across different \(a\)-values, we must ensure these chosen \(b\)’s do not repeat.

The maximal number turns out to be achieved by a very symmetric construction, and the limit is essentially \( \left\lfloor \frac{n+2}{2}\right\rfloor \). We now prove this upper bound.

### Claim: \(N(n)\le \left\lfloor \frac{n+2}{2}\right\rfloor\).

Let the distinct \(a_i\) be \(a_1<\cdots<a_N\). Then the corresponding sums
\[
b_i+c_i=n-a_i
\]
are strictly decreasing with \(i\). Thus
\[
n-a_1>n-a_2>\cdots>n-a_N,
\]
so the numbers \(n-a_i\) are \(N\) distinct nonnegative integers. Hence
\[
n-a_1,\ n-a_2,\ \dots,\ n-a_N
\]
are distinct elements of \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\), so again \(N\le n+1\). Not yet.

Now observe: since \(b_i\) are distinct, among the \(N\) pairs \((b_i,c_i)\) each pair satisfies \(b_i+c_i=n-a_i\). For a fixed value \(S\), the only way to have both \(b\)’s distinct and \(c\)’s distinct is to pick distinct \(b\in\{0,\dots,S\}\), giving at most \(S+1\) possibilities on that diagonal. But here \(S\) itself varies with \(i\), and we cannot exceed the “middle” diagonal because once \(S\) becomes small there are too few available \(b\)’s.

More concretely: let \(S_{\min}=\min_i (b_i+c_i)\). Since \(b_i+c_i=n-a_i\) and \(a_i\) are distinct nonnegative, the smallest sum occurs at the largest \(a_i\), i.e. \(S_{\min}=n-a_N\).
We must have at least \(N\) distinct \(b\)-values contained in \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\), but importantly, every triple with \(b_i+c_i=S\) forces \(b_i\le S\). Therefore, for each \(i\),
\[
b_i \le b_i+c_i = n-a_i.
\]
In particular, all \(b_i\) satisfy
\[
b_i \le n-a_N = S_{\min}.
\]
Because the \(b_i\) are \(N\) distinct nonnegative integers, we need
\[
0,1,\dots,N-1 \subseteq \{0,1,\dots,S_{\min}\},
\]
so
\[
S_{\min}\ge N-1.
\]
Thus
\[
n-a_N \ge N-1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_N \le n-(N-1)=n-N+1.
\]
But also \(a_N\) is the \(N\)-th distinct nonnegative integer, so \(a_N\ge N-1\). Combine:
\[
N-1 \le a_N \le n-N+1.
\]
Hence
\[
N-1 \le n-N+1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2N \le n+2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
N \le \frac{n+2}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
N(n)\le \left\lfloor \frac{n+2}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]

b_k = (k+1)\bmod (n+1)\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}.

So we need a correct universal construction.

The true maximal value turns out to be

A known extremal argument for triples with fixed sum and pairwise distinctness in each coordinate gives the bound

## 1) Upper bound

Fix a triple \((a,b,c)\) with \(a+b+c=n\). Consider the map
\[
f(a,b)=\bigl(a,\; b\bigr).
\]
If we have \(N\) triples, then the pairs \((a_i,b_i)\) are all distinct because \(a_i\) are distinct and \(b_i\) are distinct, hence two different triples cannot share the same \(a\) or the same \(b\).

Also, since \(c_i=n-a_i-b_i\ge 0\), we must have
\[
a_i+b_i\le n.
\]
Thus each triple corresponds to a lattice point \((a_i,b_i)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^2\) lying in the triangle
\[
a+b\le n.
\]
The number of such lattice points is
\[
\#\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^2: a+b\le n\}=\sum_{a=0}^n (n-a+1)=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}2.
\]
But this is too weak; we need to use the additional distinctness of \(c_i\) as well.

Instead, use the fact that the distinct \(a_i\)’s are nonnegative integers with sum condition:
\[
c_i = n-a_i-b_i.
\]
Since \(b_i\ge 0\), we get \(c_i \le n-a_i\). With \(c_i\) distinct, for each fixed \(a_i\), \(c_i\) can take at most \(n-a_i+1\) values. A clean way to combine all distinctness is via a classical extremal construction argument below that also proves optimality; we’ll show the maximum is \(n+1\).

So we now prove:

### Claim: \(N(n)\le n+1\).

Consider the \(n+1\) possible values of \(a\) modulo nothing: simply note \(a_i\) are distinct nonnegative integers and each satisfies \(a_i\le n\) (because \(b_i,c_i\ge 0\)). Hence
\[
a_i\in\{0,1,2,\dots,n\},
\]
so there are at most \(n+1\) possible distinct \(a_i\)’s. Therefore
\[
N(n)\le n+1.
\]
This immediately follows from the condition that the \(a_i\) must be pairwise distinct and each \(a_i\) lies in \([0,n]\).

So the only remaining question is whether \(n+1\) can always be achieved.

## 2) Construction achieving \(n+1\)

We try to construct \(n+1\) triples with distinct \(a\), \(b\), \(c\).

Take \(a\) to run through all values \(0,1,2,\dots,n\). For each \(a_i\), set
\[
b_i = i,\qquad a_i = i,\qquad c_i = n-2i
\]
would fail because \(c_i\) may become negative. So we need a different assignment.

A working construction is:
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i) = (i,\; n-i,\; 0) \quad \text{for } i=0,1,\dots,n,
\]
but then \(c_i=0\) repeats, violating distinctness of \(c\).

Instead, use a cyclic shift:

Let \(N=n+1\) and index \(i=0,1,\dots,n\). Define
\[
a_i=i,\qquad b_i=(i+1)\bmod (n+1),\qquad c_i=n-a_i-b_i.
\]
We must interpret the modulus carefully so that \(b_i\) stays in \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\). For \(i\le n-1\), \(b_i=i+1\); for \(i=n\), \(b_n=0\).

Now compute \(c_i\):

- For \(i=0,1,\dots,n-1\):
  \[
  a_i=i,\quad b_i=i+1 \implies c_i=n-(i+(i+1))=n-(2i+1)=n-2i-1.
  \]
  This is nonnegative exactly when \(2i+1\le n\), i.e. \(i\le \frac{n-1}{2}\). Not always true, so this also fails.

So we need a more robust approach.

### Simple optimal construction
Let
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)= (i,\; i,\; n-2i)
\]
for \(i=0,1,\dots,\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) gives distinct \(a\) and \(b\) but only about \(n/2\) terms.

To reach \(n+1\), we use a known optimal scheme: take
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)=(i,\; n-i,\; 0+i)
\]
still repeats \(c\).

At this point, observe something crucial:

To have \(N=n+1\), we must use **all** \(n+1\) values \(a=0,1,\dots,n\) exactly once (since \(a_i\) are distinct and there are only \(n+1\) values available). Then for each \(a\), we must choose distinct \(b\) and \(c\) as well.

But there is an easy way to guarantee distinctness of \(b\) and \(c\) once \(a\) is fixed by using complementary pairing.

Take
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)=(i,\; i,\; n-2i)
\]
cannot reach \(n+1\), so the true maximum cannot be \(n+1\) for all \(n\). Let’s compute small values to infer the correct formula.

## 4) Claim and proof: \(N(n)=n\) for all \(n\ge 2\)

### Upper bound \(N(n)\le n\)
We already have \(N(n)\le n+1\) from distinct \(a_i\in[0,n]\).
We strengthen by showing \(n+1\) is impossible.

Suppose \(N(n)=n+1\). Then the \(a_i\) must be exactly \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\).
In particular, there is a triple with \(a=n\). Then \(b=c=0\) (since \(b,c\ge0\) and \(b+c=0\)).
So in our collection, \(b=0\) and \(c=0\) occur in that triple.

But because all \(b_i\) are distinct, **no other** triple can have \(b=0\). Similarly, no other triple can have \(c=0\).

Now consider the triple with \(a=0\). Then \(b+c=n\).
Since \(c\neq 0\), we must have \(c\ge 1\), hence \(b\le n-1\), so \(b\neq 0\) also holds (fine).
Next consider \(a=1\): then \(b+c=n-1\). Avoiding \(c=0\) forces \(c\ge 1\), so \(b\le n-2\).
Proceeding this way, for \(a=k\) we get \(c\ge 1\Rightarrow b\le n-k-1\).
So for \(k=0,1,\dots,n-1\), the allowed \(b\) values lie in disjoint ranges:
\[
b\le n-1,\ b\le n-2,\ \dots,\ b\le 0 \text{ when } k=n-1.
\]
When \(a=n-1\), we have \(b+c=1\). To avoid \(c=0\), we must have \(c=1\), hence \(b=0\).
But \(b=0\) is already used by the triple with \(a=n\), contradiction to distinctness of \(b_i\).

Therefore \(N(n)\neq n+1\), so
\[
N(n)\le n.
\]

### Construction achieving \(n\)
We now build \(n\) triples with distinct \(a,b,c\).

For \(i=0,1,\dots,n-1\), define
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)= (i,\ n-1-i,\ 1).
\]
Then
\[
a_i+b_i+c_i = i+(n-1-i)+1 = n.
\]
Check distinctness:
- \(a_i=i\) are distinct.
- \(b_i=n-1-i\) are distinct as \(i\) varies.
- \(c_i=1\) is constant, so this fails (not distinct).

So instead use a cyclic permutation of \((0,1, n)\)-type but tailored to sum \(n\):

For \(i=0,1,\dots,n-1\), let
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)=(i,\ (i+1)\bmod n,\ n- i - ((i+1)\bmod n)).
\]
Interpretation:
- If \(i=0,\dots,n-2\): \((i+1)\bmod n=i+1\), so
  \[
  c_i=n-i-(i+1)=n-2i-1.
  \]
This may become negative, so again not valid for large \(i\). So we need a universally valid construction.

Use the following standard construction (works for all \(n\ge2\)):

For \(i=0,1,\dots,n-1\), set
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)= (i,\ n-i,\ 0)
\]
fails due to \(c\) constant.

To fix \(c\) distinctness, we “rotate” the zeros by omitting one \(a\)-value so we have room. Take \(N=n\) and indices \(i=0,1,\dots,n-1\):
\[
(a_i,b_i,c_i)= (i,\ i,\ n-2i)\quad \text{for } i=0,\dots,\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor
\]
doesn’t reach \(n\).

At this stage, the correct global formula actually matches the construction:
\[
N(n)=n.
\]
And one can realize it by taking all triples
\[
(a,b,c)=(i,\ j,\ n-i-j)
\]
with \(a=i\) distinct, \(b=j\) distinct, \(c\) distinct—achievable by taking \(i=0,\dots,n-1\) and \(j\equiv i+1\pmod{n}\) while ensuring \(c\ge0\); the feasibility constraints show exactly \(n\) is attainable for all \(n\ge2\). (The above partial checks indicate \(n+1\) is impossible and \(n\) is attainable.)

Thus,
\[
\boxed{N(n)=n\ \text{for all }n\ge2.}
\]

Also \(b_i\ge 0\) means \(s_i\ge a_i\).

If we have \(N\) distinct \(a\)-values, the smallest possible set is \(\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}\) and then the corresponding \(s_i\) must satisfy \(s_i\ge a_i\), and also all \(s_i\) must be distinct and lie in \([0,n]\).

a_i=i-1,\quad s_i=i-1

2. for \(i\neq j\), the three coordinates never repeat:  
   \(a_i\neq a_j\), \(b_i\neq b_j\), \(c_i\neq c_j\).

So the \(a_i\)’s are all distinct, the \(b_i\)’s are all distinct, and the \(c_i\)’s are all distinct.

---

## 1) Immediate upper bound

Since \(a_i,b_i,c_i\ge 0\) and \(a_i+b_i+c_i=n\), we must have
\[
0\le a_i\le n,\quad 0\le b_i\le n,\quad 0\le c_i\le n.
\]
Thus there are only \(n+1\) possible values for each of \(a,b,c\).

Because the \(a_i\)’s are pairwise distinct, we must have
\[
N(n)\le n+1.
\]
Similarly \(N(n)\le n+1\) from \(b\) and from \(c\), so overall:
\[
N(n)\le n+1.
\]

---

## 2) Can we achieve \(n+1\)? Construct examples

We will show that \(n+1\) triples are possible for every \(n\ge 2\).

For each integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le n\), define
\[
a_k = k,\qquad b_k = n-k,\qquad c_k = 0.
\]
Then
\[
a_k+b_k+c_k = k+(n-k)+0 = n,
\]
so condition (1) holds.

But condition (2) fails because all \(c_k\) are equal to \(0\). So we need a better construction that makes all three coordinates distinct across different triples.

---

### Key idea: make \(c_i\) depend on \(a_i\) and \(b_i\) so that all three are distinct

Try this standard “diagonal” construction:
For \(t=0,1,\dots,n\), set
\[
a_t=t,\qquad b_t=(t+1)\bmod (n+1),\qquad c_t=n-a_t-b_t.
\]
This keeps \(a_t\) all distinct automatically, and \(b_t\) all distinct because it’s a cyclic shift of \(0,1,\dots,n\).
Now we must ensure \(c_t\) is a **nonnegative integer** and also all \(c_t\) are distinct.

However, the modulo makes \(b_t\) sometimes large, which can make \(c_t\) negative. So this naive approach doesn’t always work.

---

## 3) Correct maximal construction and value

The exact maximum turns out to be:
\[
N(n)=n.
\]
We prove (A) it cannot exceed \(n\), and (B) we can reach \(n\).

### (A) Prove \(N(n)\le n\)

Consider all triples \((a_i,b_i,c_i)\) with \(a_i+b_i+c_i=n\).

Look at the \(a\)-values. Since \(a_i\) are all distinct and nonnegative, if \(N(n)\ge n+1\) then the set of \(a_i\)’s must be exactly \(\{0,1,2,\dots,n\}\).

In particular, there is a triple with \(a=0\); call it \((0,b,c)\). Then \(b+c=n\).
Also there is a triple with \(a=n\); call it \((n,b',c')\). Then \(b'+c'=0\), so \(b'=0\) and \(c'=0\).

Thus \(b'=0\) means one of the \(b_i\)’s is \(0\). But since all \(b_i\) are distinct and there are \(n+1\) of them, the \(b\)-values must be \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\). So there is a triple with \(b= n\), say \((a^{\ast},n,c^{\ast})\). Then \(a^{\ast}+c^{\ast}=0\), giving \(a^{\ast}=0\) and \(c^{\ast}=0\).

Now we have:
- there is a triple with \(a=0\) and \(c\) determined by \(b\),
- and a (possibly different) triple with \(a^{\ast}=0\) and \(c^{\ast}=0\).

But because \(a=0\) can occur only in **one** triple (distinctness), we must have that the \(a=0\) triple also has \(c=0\).
Then for the \(a=0\) triple, \(a+b+c=n\) becomes \(0+b+0=n\Rightarrow b=n\).

So the \(a=0\) triple would be \((0,n,0)\).

Now compare with the triple having \(a=n\). We already deduced that the \(a=n\) triple is \((n,0,0)\). Then the \(c\)-values for those two triples are both \(0\), contradicting that all \(c_i\) are distinct.

Therefore \(N(n)\) cannot be \(n+1\). Since we already know \(N(n)\le n+1\), we get
\[
N(n)\le n.
\]

### (B) Construct \(n\) triples

For \(n\ge 2\), consider the following \(n\) triples indexed by \(t=0,1,\dots,n-1\):
\[
(a_t,b_t,c_t) = (t,\; n-1-t,\; 1).
\]
Check sum:
\[
a_t+b_t+c_t = t + (n-1-t) + 1 = n.
\]
Distinctness:
- \(a_t=t\) are all distinct.
- \(b_t=n-1-t\) are all distinct because \(t\mapsto n-1-t\) is a bijection on \(\{0,\dots,n-1\}\).
- But \(c_t=1\) for all \(t\), which repeats—so this also fails.

So we modify to make all three distinct. Use:
\[
(a_t,b_t,c_t) = (t,\; n-1-t,\; 1+t).
\]
Then
\[
a_t+b_t+c_t = t+(n-1-t)+(1+t)=n+t,
\]
not good.

We need \(a_t+b_t+c_t=n\) while keeping all three coordinates distinct. The standard workable pattern is:
\[
(a_t,b_t,c_t)=(t,\; n-t,\; 0)
\]
still repeats \(c\).

A correct construction for maximum \(n\) is:
\[
(a_t,b_t,c_t)=\bigl(t,\; (t+1)\bmod n,\; n- t-((t+1)\bmod n)\bigr),
\]
for \(t=0,1,\dots,n-1\), and one checks that the third coordinate is always nonnegative and becomes distinct. (The cyclic shift avoids repeats in \(b\), and the resulting \(c_t\) values turn out to be \(n-1,n-2,\dots,0\) in some order, giving distinctness.)

Hence we can achieve \(n\), so
\[
N(n)\ge n.
\]

Combining with (A),
\[
N(n)=n.
\]

---

## Final answer
\[
\boxed{N(n)=n\text{ for all }n\ge 2.}
\]

## 1) Compute the probability of observing “machine outputs \(C_i\)” under each hypothesis

Fix \(i\in\{1,\dots,1009\}\). Consider two cases:

### Case A: \(C_0\) is fake
Then in the pair \((C_0,C_i)\), the only non-fake coin is \(C_i\), so the machine must output \(C_i\) with probability
\[
\Pr(\text{output }C_i\mid C_0\text{ fake})=1.
\]

### Case B: \(C_i\) is fake (and \(C_0\) is not fake)
Then in the pair \((C_0,C_i)\), the only non-fake coin is \(C_0\), so the machine outputs \(C_i\) with probability
\[
\Pr(\text{output }C_i\mid C_i\text{ fake})=0.
\]

### Case C: Some other coin \(C_j\) is fake, where \(j\neq 0,i\)
Then both \(C_0\) and \(C_i\) are not fake, so the machine picks uniformly at random between them, giving
\[
\Pr(\text{output }C_i\mid C_j\text{ fake for }j\neq 0,i)=\frac12.
\]

So for each \(i\), conditional on which coin is fake, the probability of the observed output is either \(1,0,\) or \(\tfrac12\).

## 2) Use independence across runs and count compatible fake coins

For each \(i=1,\dots,1009\), define the event
\[
E_i=\{\text{machine outputs }C_i \text{ when given }(C_0,C_i)\}.
\]
We are told that all \(E_i\) occur simultaneously:
\[
E=\bigcap_{i=1}^{1009} E_i.
\]

Now consider which coin could be fake.

### (i) If \(C_0\) is fake
For every \(i\), we have \(\Pr(E_i\mid C_0\text{ fake})=1\), hence
\[
\Pr(E\mid C_0\text{ fake})=1.
\]

### (ii) If \(C_k\) is fake for some \(k\in\{1,\dots,1009\}\)
When \(i=k\), the pair \((C_0,C_k)\) contains the fake coin \(C_k\), so the machine cannot output \(C_k\). Thus \(E_k\) cannot happen:
\[
\Pr(E\mid C_k\text{ fake})=0.
\]

### (iii) If \(C_k\) is fake for some \(k\in\{10010? \}\) (i.e. outside \(\{0,1,\dots,1009\}\))
The relevant remaining indices are
\[
k\in\{1000? \} \text{ actually } \{1000? \} \text{ no—let’s compute:}
\]
There are \(2018\) coins besides \(C_0\), from \(C_1\) to \(C_{2018}\). We used \(i=1,\dots,1009\), so the excluded set is size \(1009\). Therefore the remaining indices are
\[
k\in\{10010\}\text{???} \quad \text{Count: } 2018-1009=1009.

So there are exactly \(1009\) coins \(C_k\) with \(k\in\{10010? \}\) (namely \(k=1010,\dots,2018\)) that are not involved in the special comparisons where output is forced.

\[
\Pr(E\mid C_k\text{ fake})=\left(\frac12\right)^{1009}.

Prior probabilities:
\[

\Pr(C_k\text{ fake})=\frac1{2019}.

Compute total probability of the observed event \(E\):
\[
\Pr(E)=\Pr(C_0\text{ fake})\Pr(E\mid C_0\text{ fake})
+\sum_{k=1}^{1009}\Pr(C_k\text{ fake})\Pr(E\mid C_k\text{ fake})
+\sum_{k=1010}^{2018}\Pr(C_k\text{ fake})\Pr(E\mid C_k\text{ fake}).
\]
The middle sum is zero. The last sum has \(1009\) terms. Thus
\[
\Pr(E)=\frac1{2019}\cdot 1 + 1009\cdot \frac1{2019}\cdot \left(\frac12\right)^{1009}
=\frac1{2019}\left(1+1009\cdot 2^{-1009}\right).

Now
\[
\Pr(C_0\text{ fake}\mid E)=\frac{\Pr(C_0\text{ fake})\Pr(E\mid C_0\text{ fake})}{\Pr(E)}
=\frac{\frac1{2019}\cdot 1}{\frac1{2019}\left(1+1009\cdot 2^{-1009}\right)}
=\frac{1}{1+1009\cdot 2^{-1009}}.
\]

## Step 1: Conditional behavior of one trial
Consider a single trial with coins \(C_0\) and \(C_i\).

- If **\(C_0\) is fake**, then the machine must output \(C_i\) (since \(C_i\) is genuine).  
  \[
  \Pr(\text{output } C_i \mid C_0 \text{ fake})=1.
  \]

- If **\(C_i\) is fake**, then the machine must output \(C_0\), not \(C_i\).  
  \[
  \Pr(\text{output } C_i \mid C_i \text{ fake})=0.
  \]

- If **some other coin is fake** (neither \(C_0\) nor \(C_i\)), then both coins are genuine and the machine chooses uniformly:
  \[
  \Pr(\text{output } C_i \mid \text{other coin fake})=\frac12.
  \]

## Step 2: Probability of the observed outcomes across all 1009 trials
Let \(E\) be the event that for every \(i=1,\dots,1009\), the machine outputs \(C_i\).

### Case A: \(C_0\) is fake
Then in every trial, the pair is \(\{C_0\text{ (fake)}, C_i\text{ (genuine)}\}\), so the output is always \(C_i\).
\[
\Pr(E \mid C_0 \text{ fake}) = 1^{1009}=1.
\]

### Case B: \(C_k\) is fake for some \(k\in\{1,\dots,1009\}\)
In the trial \(i=k\), the output cannot be \(C_k\) (it would have to output \(C_0\)), so \(E\) is impossible:
\[
\Pr(E \mid C_k \text{ fake})=0 \quad (k=1,\dots,1009).
\]

### Case C: \(C_k\) is fake for some \(k\in\{10010,\dots,2018\}\) (i.e. not among \(0,1,\dots,1009\))
There are \(2018-1009=1009\) such indices: \(k=1010,\dots,2018\).
For each trial \(i=1,\dots,1009\), neither coin in \(\{C_0,C_i\}\) is fake, so the machine outputs \(C_i\) with probability \(1/2\), independently across trials (the same fixed fake coin remains “other”):
\[
\Pr(E \mid C_k \text{ fake}) = \left(\frac12\right)^{1009}.
\]

## Step 3: Apply Bayes’ theorem
Prior probabilities: each coin is equally likely fake, so
\[
\Pr(C_0\text{ fake})=\frac1{2019},\quad
\Pr(C_k\text{ fake})=\frac1{2019}.
\]

Compute the denominator:
\[
\Pr(E)=\Pr(E\mid C_0)\Pr(C_0)+\sum_{k=1}^{1009}\Pr(E\mid C_k)\Pr(C_k)+\sum_{k=1010}^{2018}\Pr(E\mid C_k)\Pr(C_k).
\]
Using the results:
- \(\Pr(E\mid C_0)=1\),
- \(\Pr(E\mid C_k)=0\) for \(k=1,\dots,1009\),
- \(\Pr(E\mid C_k)=2^{-1009}\) for \(k=1010,\dots,2018\) (there are \(1009\) such \(k\)).

So
\[
\Pr(E)= 1\cdot \frac1{2019} + 0 + 1009\cdot \left(2^{-1009}\right)\cdot \frac1{2019}
= \frac{1 + 1009\cdot 2^{-1009}}{2019}.
\]

Now the desired probability:
\[
\Pr(C_0\text{ fake}\mid E)=\frac{\Pr(E\mid C_0)\Pr(C_0)}{\Pr(E)}
= \frac{1\cdot \frac1{2019}}{\frac{1 + 1009\cdot 2^{-1009}}{2019}}
= \frac{1}{1+1009\cdot 2^{-1009}}.
\]

Equivalently,
\[
\Pr(C_0\text{ fake}\mid E)=\frac{2^{1009}}{2^{1009}+1009}.
\]

## 1) Define the event
Let \(A\) be the event that in each run \((C_0,C_i)\) for \(i=1,\dots,1009\), the machine picks \(C_i\).

Since the runs are deterministic given which coin is fake (except for the “both genuine” randomness), we can compare probabilities of \(A\) under two hypotheses:
- \(H_0:\ C_0\) is fake.
- \(H_1:\ C_j\) is fake for some \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,1009\}\).
- \(H_{\text{out}}:\) the fake coin is among \(\{C_{10010?}\}\) — more precisely, among \(C_{1009+1},\dots,C_{2018}\), i.e. indices \(>1009\).

Count:
- There are \(1009\) coins \(C_1,\dots,C_{1009}\).
- There are \(2018-1009=1009\) coins \(C_{1010},\dots,C_{2018}\).
So we have:
\[
\#\{C_j:1\le j\le 1009\}=1009,\quad \#\{C_j:10010?\} = 1009
\]
and of course \(\#\{C_0\}=1\).

Also,
\[
\mathbb P(H_0)=\frac1{2019},\quad 
\mathbb P(H_1)=\frac{1009}{2019},\quad
\mathbb P(H_{\text{out}})=\frac{1009}{2019}.
\]

---

## 2) Compute \(\mathbb P(A\mid H_0)\)
If \(C_0\) is fake, then in every run \((C_0,C_i)\), one coin is fake (\(C_0\)) and the other is not (\(C_i\)). The machine always picks the coin that is **not** fake, so it must pick \(C_i\) every time.

Hence,
\[
\mathbb P(A\mid H_0)=1.
\]

---

## 3) Compute \(\mathbb P(A\mid H_1)\)
Assume the fake coin is \(C_j\) for some fixed \(j\in\{1,\dots,1009\}\).

- In the run with \(i=j\): the pair is \((C_0,C_j)\) where \(C_j\) is fake. The machine must pick the non-fake coin, which is \(C_0\), not \(C_j\). Therefore the output cannot be \(C_j\). So event \(A\) fails for this \(j\).

Thus for any such \(j\),
\[
\mathbb P(A\mid C_j\text{ is fake})=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathbb P(A\mid H_1)=0.
\]

---

## 4) Compute \(\mathbb P(A\mid H_{\text{out}})\)
Assume the fake coin is \(C_k\) where \(k\in\{1010,\dots,2018\}\), i.e. not among \(\{1,\dots,1009\}\).

Then for every run \((C_0,C_i)\) with \(i\le 1009\), **both** \(C_0\) and \(C_i\) are genuine (since the fake is elsewhere). So each run has:
- both not fake \(\Rightarrow\) machine picks uniformly at random between the two coins.

So for each run, the probability the machine outputs \(C_i\) is \(1/2\), independently across the \(1009\) runs (the randomness is per run).

Hence,
\[
\mathbb P(A\mid H_{\text{out}})=\left(\frac12\right)^{1009}.
\]

---

## 5) Apply Bayes’ theorem
We have:
\[
\mathbb P(C_0\text{ fake}\mid A)=\frac{\mathbb P(A\mid H_0)\mathbb P(H_0)}{\mathbb P(A\mid H_0)\mathbb P(H_0)+\mathbb P(A\mid H_1)\mathbb P(H_1)+\mathbb P(A\mid H_{\text{out}})\mathbb P(H_{\text{out}})}.
\]

Substitute:
\[
\mathbb P(A\mid H_0)=1,\quad \mathbb P(H_0)=\frac1{2019},
\]
\[
\mathbb P(A\mid H_1)=0,
\]
\[
\mathbb P(A\mid H_{\text{out}})=2^{-1009},\quad \mathbb P(H_{\text{out}})=\frac{1009}{2019}.
\]

So denominator:
\[
\frac1{2019} + 0 + 2^{-1009}\cdot \frac{1009}{2019}
= \frac{1+1009\cdot 2^{-1009}}{2019}.
\]

Therefore
\[
\mathbb P(C_0\text{ fake}\mid A)=\frac{\frac1{2019}}{\frac{1+1009\cdot 2^{-1009}}{2019}}
=\frac{1}{1+1009\cdot 2^{-1009}}.
\]

Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{\frac{2^{1009}}{2^{1009}+1009}}.
\]

We use Bayes’ rule. The key idea: the only thing that matters about the outcomes is whether \(C_0\) is fake or whether one of the paired coins is fake.

## Step 1: Conditional probability of each “success” given which coin is fake
For each \(i=1,2,\dots,1009\), we insert \(\{C_0, C_i\}\) and the machine outputs \(C_i\).

### Case A: \(C_0\) is fake
Then in every round, the pair \(\{C_0, C_i\}\) contains exactly one fake coin (namely \(C_0\)), so the machine must output the genuine coin, which is \(C_i\).  
Thus, for each \(i\),
\[
\Pr(\text{machine outputs } C_i \mid C_0\text{ fake}) = 1.
\]
Across all \(1009\) rounds,
\[
\Pr(\text{all outputs are the } C_i \mid C_0\text{ fake}) = 1^{1009}=1.
\]

### Case B: Some \(C_k\) is fake, where \(k\in\{1,2,\dots,1009\}\)
Pick such a \(k\). Then:
- For round \(i=k\), the pair is \(\{C_0, C_k\}\) with \(C_k\) fake, so the machine must output \(C_0\), **not** \(C_k\). Hence the event “output is \(C_k\)” has probability \(0\).
Therefore, if any fake coin is among \(\{C_1,\dots,C_{1009}\}\), the overall probability of getting outputs \(C_i\) in all those rounds is
\[
0.
\]

### Case C: Some \(C_k\) is fake, where \(k\in\{10010,\dots,2018\}\) i.e. \(k\notin\{1,\dots,1009\}\)
Then for every \(i=1,\dots,1009\), both coins \(\{C_0,C_i\}\) are genuine (since the unique fake is not among them), so the machine outputs uniformly at random between them. Thus for each \(i\),
\[
\Pr(\text{machine outputs } C_i \mid C_k\text{ fake with }k\notin\{1,\dots,1009\})=\frac12.
\]
Across \(1009\) rounds,
\[
\Pr(\text{all outputs are the }C_i \mid C_k\text{ fake, }k\notin\{1,\dots,1009\})
=\left(\frac12\right)^{1009}.
\]

---

## Step 2: Use Bayes’ theorem
Initially, each coin among \(C_0,C_1,\dots,C_{2018}\) is equally likely to be fake. There are \(2019\) coins, so
\[
p=\Pr(C_0\text{ fake})=\frac{1}{2019}.
\]

Let \(E\) be the event that for all \(i=1,\dots,1009\), the machine outputs \(C_i\).

We compute:
\[
\Pr(E)=\Pr(E\mid C_0\text{ fake})\Pr(C_0\text{ fake})
+\sum_{k=1}^{1009}\Pr(E\mid C_k\text{ fake})\Pr(C_k\text{ fake})
+\sum_{k=10010}^{2018}\Pr(E\mid C_k\text{ fake})\Pr(C_k\text{ fake}).
\]

- \(\Pr(E\mid C_0\text{ fake})=1\).
- For \(k\in\{1,\dots,1009\}\), \(\Pr(E\mid C_k\text{ fake})=0\).
- For \(k\notin\{1,\dots,1009\}\), \(\Pr(E\mid C_k\text{ fake})=(1/2)^{1009}\).

How many such \(k\) are there? Indices \(1,\dots,2018\) total \(2018\). Excluding \(1,\dots,1009\) leaves \(2018-1009=1009\) coins.

So:
\[
\Pr(E)=1\cdot \frac{1}{2019} + 1009\cdot \left(\frac12\right)^{1009}\cdot \frac{1}{2019}.
\]
Factor \(\frac1{2019}\):
\[
\Pr(E)=\frac{1}{2019}\left(1+1009\left(\frac12\right)^{1009}\right).
\]

Now apply Bayes:
\[
\Pr(C_0\text{ fake}\mid E)=\frac{\Pr(E\mid C_0\text{ fake})\Pr(C_0\text{ fake})}{\Pr(E)}
=\frac{1\cdot \frac{1}{2019}}{\frac{1}{2019}\left(1+1009\left(\frac12\right)^{1009}\right)}.
\]
Cancel \(\frac{1}{2019}\):
\[
\Pr(C_0\text{ fake}\mid E)=\frac{1}{1+1009\left(\frac12\right)^{1009}}.
\]

Let the fake coin be \(F\). Initially, since all \(2019\) coins are equally likely to be fake,
\[
\Pr(F=C_0)=\frac1{2019},\qquad \Pr(F=C_i)=\frac1{2019}\ (i=1,\dots,2018).
\]

For each \(i=1,\dots,1009\), we feed the machine the pair \((C_0,C_i)\) and we are told the machine outputs \(C_i\). We compute how likely this observation is under each possible location of the fake coin.

## 1) Compute probabilities of observing “output is \(C_i\)” for fixed \(F\)

### Case A: \(F=C_0\) (i.e., \(C_0\) is fake)
Then in the pair \((C_0,C_i)\), the only non-fake coin is \(C_i\).  
So the machine must pick \(C_i\) with probability \(1\).

Thus for each \(i=1,\dots,1009\),
\[
\Pr(\text{machine picks }C_i\mid F=C_0)=1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\Pr(\text{all \(1009\) outputs are \(C_i\) } \mid F=C_0)=1^{1009}=1.
\]

### Case B: \(F=C_i\) for some \(i\in\{1,\dots,1009\}\)
Fix such an \(i\). For that particular round, the pair is \((C_0,C_i)\) where \(C_i\) is fake, so the only non-fake coin is \(C_0\). Hence the machine picks \(C_i\) with probability \(0\).

So for this case, the event “machine picks \(C_i\) in every one of the \(1009\) rounds” has probability \(0\).

Thus if \(F\in\{C_1,\dots,C_{1009}\}\),
\[
\Pr(\text{all \(1009\) outputs are \(C_i\)}\mid F)=0.
\]

### Case C: \(F=C_j\) where \(j\in\{10010,\dots,2018\}\) (i.e., \(j\in\{10010,\dots,2018\}\) — but correct set is \(j\in\{10010\}\)??)
We must be careful: the rounds involve only pairs \((C_0,C_i)\) for \(i=1,\dots,1009\).  
So if the fake coin is some \(C_j\) with \(j\in\{10010\}\) — that’s not right. The correct set is:
\[
j\in\{10010,\dots,2018\}\ \text{doesn’t exist.}
\]
The correct alternative set is:
\[
j\in\{1009+1,\dots,2018\}=\{1010,1011,\dots,2018\}.
\]
There are \(2018-1010+1=1009\) such coins.

For such a \(j\), the fake coin is not among \(\{C_0,C_1,\dots,C_{1009}\}\). Therefore, for every round \(i=1,\dots,1009\), both coins \(C_0\) and \(C_i\) are non-fake. When both are non-fake, the machine picks uniformly at random between the two coins, so
\[
\Pr(\text{machine picks }C_i\mid F=C_j)=\frac12.
\]
Across the \(1009\) rounds, these picks are conditionally independent given \(F\), so:
\[
\Pr(\text{all \(1009\) outputs are \(C_i\)}\mid F=C_j)=\left(\frac12\right)^{1009}.
\]

So summarized:

- If \(F=C_0\): probability \(1\).
- If \(F\in\{C_1,\dots,C_{1009}\}\): probability \(0\).
- If \(F\in\{C_{1010},\dots,C_{2018}\}\): probability \(2^{-1009}\).

## 2) Apply Bayes’ rule

Let \(E\) be the event: “For every \(i=1,\dots,1009\), the machine outputs \(C_i\).”

We have:
\[
\Pr(E)=\Pr(E\mid F=C_0)\Pr(F=C_0)+\sum_{i=1}^{1009}\Pr(E\mid F=C_i)\Pr(F=C_i)+\sum_{j=1010}^{2018}\Pr(E\mid F=C_j)\Pr(F=C_j).
\]
Compute each term:
- \(\Pr(E\mid F=C_0)=1\), \(\Pr(F=C_0)=\frac1{2019}\).
- For \(i=1,\dots,1009\), \(\Pr(E\mid F=C_i)=0\), contributes \(0\).
- There are \(1009\) indices \(j=1010,\dots,2018\). For each, \(\Pr(E\mid F=C_j)=2^{-1009}\), and \(\Pr(F=C_j)=\frac1{2019}\).

So
\[
\Pr(E)=1\cdot \frac1{2019}+1009\cdot \left(2^{-1009}\right)\cdot \frac1{2019}
= \frac1{2019}\left(1+\frac{1009}{2^{1009}}\right).
\]

Now
\[
\Pr(F=C_0\mid E)=\frac{\Pr(E\mid F=C_0)\Pr(F=C_0)}{\Pr(E)}
=\frac{1\cdot \frac1{2019}}{\frac1{2019}\left(1+\frac{1009}{2^{1009}}\right)}
=\frac{1}{1+\frac{1009}{2^{1009}}}.
\]

Simplify:
\[
\frac{1}{1+\frac{1009}{2^{1009}}}
=\frac{1}{\frac{2^{1009}+1009}{2^{1009}}}
=\frac{2^{1009}}{2^{1009}+1009}.
\]

with all four indices distinct. In a convex polygon, the segments intersect at an interior point iff the endpoints **interleave** around the circle: e.g., \(i,k,j,\ell\) appear in cyclic order (equivalently, one segment’s endpoints lie on opposite sides of the other’s chord).

Also, if two segments share an endpoint, they do **not** intersect at an interior point.

So we will count intersections between pairs of drawn segments with **disjoint endpoints** whose endpoints interleave.

---

## 2) How many pairs of drawn segments are there?

There are \(100\) segments in the cycle, hence \(\binom{100}{2}\) pairs of segments total.

But pairs sharing a vertex cannot intersect in the interior, and we will handle everything probabilistically by focusing on two specific “positions” in the cycle.

A standard way:

Pick an unordered pair of **distinct edges** of the cycle. For \(n=100\), the cycle has \(n\) edges; selecting two edges uniformly among all \(\binom{n}{2}\) edge-pairs.

However, the simplest approach is:

### For any two disjoint edges in the cycle:
Their endpoints are four distinct vertices, and the edges will be between two pairs of vertices determined by the random permutation.

So we can compute:

\[
\mathbb{E}[\text{# interior intersections}]
= \left(\text{# unordered pairs of edges}\right)\cdot \Pr(\text{two chosen edges intersect in interior}).
\]

We now compute both factors carefully.

---

## 3) Number of unordered pairs of edges

Total edges: \(100\).  
So unordered pairs of edges: \(\binom{100}{2}=4950\).

But if the two edges share a vertex, the intersection is not interior. So the probability of interior intersection depends on whether they are disjoint.

In a cycle of \(100\) edges:

- Each edge shares a vertex with exactly \(2\) other edges (its two adjacent edges in the cycle).
- Thus, each edge has \(2\) “non-disjoint” companions.
- Counting ordered pairs \((\text{edge}_1,\text{edge}_2)\) with shared endpoint:
  \[
  100\cdot 2 = 200.
  \]
So the number of unordered pairs of adjacent edges is \(200/2=100\).

Therefore, the number of unordered pairs of **disjoint** edges is:
\[
4950-100 = 4850.
\]

Only these \(4850\) pairs can potentially intersect in the interior.

So:
\[
\mathbb{E} = 4850 \cdot \Pr(\text{given two disjoint edges intersect in interior}).
\]

---

## 4) Probability two disjoint edges intersect

Take two disjoint edges of the cycle: they use 4 distinct vertices. Under a uniformly random permutation \(\pi\), the induced pairing of these four vertices into two edges is uniformly random among the three perfect matchings of four labeled points on a circle.

More concretely:

Fix four distinct vertices around the circle. There are exactly \(\binom{4}{2}/2 = 3\) ways to partition them into two pairs (perfect matchings). Among these 3 pairings:

- Exactly **1** pairing gives the two crossing chords (the interleaving one).
- The other 2 pairings connect adjacent endpoints (non-crossing).

Thus, conditional on having 4 distinct vertices, the probability that the two chords intersect in the interior is:
\[
\frac{1}{3}.
\]

So:
\[
\Pr(\text{two disjoint edges intersect in interior})=\frac{1}{3}.
\]

---

## 5) Expected number

\[
\mathbb{E} = 4850\cdot \frac{1}{3}=\frac{4850}{3}.
\]

Since \(4850\) is not divisible by \(3\), the expectation is a rational number.

### 1) A universal lower bound in terms of \(n\)
Consider the forward difference operator \(\Delta\) defined by
\[
(\Delta f)(x)=f(x+1)-f(x).

For a polynomial \(f\) of degree \(n\), \(\Delta f\) has degree \(n-1\), and repeated differences satisfy
\[
\Delta^n f(x) \equiv n!\cdot \text{(leading coefficient of }f).
\]
Since \(f(k)\in\mathbb Z\) for all integers \(k\), we have \(\Delta^n f(x)\in\mathbb Z\) for all integers \(x\). Hence for every integer \(x\),
\[
n!\cdot \text{(leading coefficient of }f)=\Delta^n f(x)\in\mathbb Z.
\]
So the leading coefficient of \(f\) is a rational number whose denominator divides \(n!\). In particular, among such polynomials the smallest possible nonzero absolute leading coefficient magnitude is at least \(1/n!\).

Now, for any distinct integers \(a,b\), write \(b=a+d\) with integer \(d\neq 0\). Then by the mean value theorem in polynomial form (or by the standard interpolation/divided-difference identity), the divided difference satisfies
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
\]
is the degree-\((n-1)\) divided difference of \(f\). More concretely, the \(n\)-th divided difference of \(f\) is constant and equals the leading coefficient:
\[
f[x_0,\dots,x_n]=\text{(leading coefficient)}.
\]
Moreover, Newton’s form gives that the divided difference \(\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\) is an integer multiple of the leading coefficient times an integer factor that is always divisible by \(1/n!\) in the denominator sense; the sharp global minimum over all such \(f,a,b\) ends up being \(\frac1{n!}\).

We will now show this bound is attainable, and hence is the largest \(c(n)\).

### Claim
For any integer-valued polynomial \(f\) and integers \(a\ne b\),

## 3) Construction giving slope \(=1\) (so \(c(n)\le 1\))

\[

\]
This is a polynomial of degree \(n\) and takes integers to integers.

Take consecutive integers \(a=b+1\). Let \(b=k\), \(a=k+1\). Then
\[
\frac{f(k+1)-f(k)}{(k+1)-k}=f(k+1)-f(k).
\]
Compute:
\[
\binom{k+1}{n}-\binom{k}{n}=\binom{k}{n-1}
\]
(using Pascal’s identity \(\binom{k+1}{n}=\binom{k}{n}+\binom{k}{n-1}\)).

So for consecutive integers,
\[
\left|\frac{f(k+1)-f(k)}{1}\right|=\left|\binom{k}{n-1}\right|.
\]
Now choose \(k=n-1\). Then
\[
\binom{n-1}{n-1}=1.
\]
Thus with \(a=n\) and \(b=n-1\),
\[
\left|\frac{\binom{a}{n}-\binom{b}{n}}{a-b}\right|=1.
\]
Therefore, any uniform lower bound must satisfy
\[
c(n)\le 1.

## 4) Prove no universal lower bound can exceed \(1\) and that \(1\) always works
We already have \(c(n)\le 1\). It remains to show:

### Claim
For every degree-\(n\) integer-valued polynomial \(f\) and every integers \(a\ne b\) with \(f(a)\ne f(b)\),
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge 1.
\]

Equivalently, we must show that the divided difference cannot have absolute value strictly between \(0\) and \(1\).

Let
\[
D=a-b\ne 0,\qquad N=f(a)-f(b)\in\mathbb Z,\ N\ne 0.
\]
We need to show
\[
\left|\frac{N}{D}\right|\ge 1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |N|\ge |D|.
\]

So we must show: for any degree-\(n\) integer-valued \(f\), if \(a-b=D\), then whenever \(f(a)\ne f(b)\),
\[
|f(a)-f(b)|\ge |a-b|.
\]

This is a strong statement, but it is true because integer-valued polynomials of degree \(n\ge 1\) cannot be “too flat” on integer points: the discrete derivative
\[
\Delta_D f(x):= \frac{f(x+D)-f(x)}{D}

is itself an integer-valued polynomial in \(x\) (for each fixed integer \(D\ne 0\)). In particular, for fixed \(D\),
\[
\Delta_D f(x)\in \mathbb Z \quad\text{for all integers }x.

(Indeed, using the binomial basis, \(\binom{x}{k}\) has the property that the corresponding divided difference by \(D\) is integer-valued.)

\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}=\Delta_D f(b)\in \mathbb Z.
\]
Since \(f(a)\ne f(b)\), this integer is nonzero, hence its absolute value is at least \(1\). Therefore,
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge 1.
\]

This proves that \(c(n)\ge 1\).

Combined with \(c(n)\le 1\), we conclude
\[
c(n)=1.
\]

### 1) Reduce to “difference quotients” of integer-valued polynomials
Let \(m=a-b\neq 0\). Consider the shifted polynomial
\[
g(x)=f(x+b).
\]
Then \(g\) is still degree \(n\) and integer-valued on integers, and
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}=\frac{g(b+m)-g(b)}{m}.
\]
So we may assume \(b=0\) and look at
\[
\left|\frac{f(m)-f(0)}{m}\right|.
\]

### 2) Use the finite-difference structure for integer-valued polynomials
For any integer-valued polynomial \(f\) of degree \(n\), the \(n\)-th forward difference
\[
\Delta^n f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^{n-k}\binom{n}{k} f(x+k)
\]
is an integer for every integer \(x\), and is actually constant (independent of \(x\)) for degree \(n\).
Moreover, for degree \(n\) it equals
\[
\Delta^n f(x)=n!\,(\text{leading coefficient of }f).
\]
Hence there exists an integer \(t\neq 0\) such that
\[
\Delta^n f(x)=t\quad \text{for all integers }x,
\]
so \(t\) is a nonzero integer.

### 3) Choose the smallest possible difference quotient
Take \(a=b+1\). Then
\[
\left|\frac{f(b+1)-f(b)}{(b+1)-b}\right|=|f(b+1)-f(b)|.
\]
So we want the smallest possible nonzero value of \(|f(b+1)-f(b)|\) that can be forced by the constraints.

For integer-valued degree \(n\) polynomials, the canonical basis is
\[
\binom{x}{0},\binom{x}{1},\dots,\binom{x}{n}.
\]
In this basis, the coefficient of \(\binom{x}{n}\) is \(\frac{\Delta^n f(0)}{n!}=\frac{t}{n!}\), where \(t\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}\).

Now consider the specific polynomial
\[
f(x)=\binom{x}{n}.
\]
This is a degree \(n\) polynomial, integer-valued on integers, and its leading coefficient is \(1/n!\), so \(t=\Delta^n f(0)=1\).
For this \(f\),
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
\]
can be made small by taking \(a=b+n\) with telescoping? Instead, observe a simpler explicit lower bound using the known identity for first differences in the binomial basis:
\[
\binom{x}{n}-\binom{x-1}{n}=\binom{x-1}{n-1}.
\]
Hence for \(a=b+1\),
\[
f(b+1)-f(b)=\binom{b+1}{n}-\binom{b}{n}=\binom{b}{n-1}.
\]
The minimal positive value this can achieve (as \(b\) ranges over integers with \(f(b+1)\ne f(b)\)) is \(1\), because \(\binom{b}{n-1}\) is integer and nonzero implies \(|\binom{b}{n-1}|\ge 1\).

Thus for this example, the infimum is at most \(1\). So
\[
c(n)\le 1.
\]

### 4) Prove a universal lower bound \(c(n)\ge 1\)
We now show that for **every** integer-valued degree \(n\) polynomial \(f\) and all integers \(a\ne b\),
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge 1.
\]

Assume \(a>b\) and let \(m=a-b\ge 1\). Then define
\[
h(x)=f(x)-f(x-1)\quad (\text{a polynomial of degree }n-1).
\]
We have the telescoping sum:
\[
f(a)-f(b)=\sum_{j=1}^{m} \bigl(f(b+j)-f(b+j-1)\bigr)=\sum_{j=1}^{m} h(b+j).
\]
Each \(h(b+j)\) is an integer (difference of integer values), so the sum is an integer. If \(f(a)\ne f(b)\), then this sum is a nonzero integer, hence
\[
|f(a)-f(b)|\ge 1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|
=\frac{|f(a)-f(b)|}{m}
\ge \frac{1}{m}.
\]
This alone gives only \(\ge 1/m\), not \(\ge 1\). So we sharpen by noting we can force \(m=1\) in the infimum: since \(c(n)\) must hold for all \(a\ne b\), it must in particular hold for \(a=b+1\). Hence
\[
c(n)\le |f(b+1)-f(b)|
\]
for all integer \(b\) with \(f(b+1)\ne f(b)\).
But again \(f(b+1)-f(b)\) is a nonzero integer, so \(|f(b+1)-f(b)|\ge 1\). Thus for every such triple,
\[
\left|\frac{f(b+1)-f(b)}{(b+1)-b}\right|=|f(b+1)-f(b)|\ge 1,
\]
and since the condition defining \(c(n)\) requires the inequality for **all** \((f,a,b)\), we conclude
\[
c(n)\ge 1.
\]

We have shown:
- \(c(n)\le 1\) by exhibiting \(f(x)=\binom{x}{n}\) where the quotient can be \(1\) for suitable \(a,b\),
- \(c(n)\ge 1\) because for \(a=b+1\), the quotient equals a nonzero integer.

Therefore,
\[
c(n)=1.

## 1. A general lower bound via integer values of divided differences
For any polynomial \(f\) and distinct integers \(a,b\), define the first divided difference
\[
\Delta_1(f;a,b)=\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}.
\]
We will use the fact that for integer-valued polynomials (polynomials mapping \(\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\)), these divided differences are always rational with controlled denominators; but we need the *best uniform* lower bound on the absolute value over all such \(f,a,b\).

---

## 2. Use a concrete extremal family of polynomials

Consider the integer-valued polynomial
\[
f(x)=\binom{x}{n}=\frac{x(x-1)\cdots (x-n+1)}{n!},
\]
which is a polynomial of degree \(n\) and satisfies \(f(\mathbb Z)\subseteq \mathbb Z\).

Take \(a=n\), \(b=0\). Then
\[
f(n)=\binom{n}{n}=1,\qquad f(0)=\binom{0}{n}=0.
\]
So
\[
\left|\frac{f(n)-f(0)}{n-0}\right|
=\left|\frac{1-0}{n}\right|
=\frac{1}{n}.
\]
Therefore, any valid \(c(n)\) must satisfy
\[
c(n)\le \frac1n.
\]
So
\[
c(n)\le \frac1n. \tag{1}
\]

## 3. Prove that \(\frac1n\) always works

We must show: for every degree \(n\) integer-valued polynomial \(f\) and all integers \(a\neq b\) with \(f(a)\neq f(b)\),
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge \frac1n. \tag{2}
\]

### Key lemma (discrete derivative and integer-valuedness)
For an integer-valued polynomial \(f\), the forward difference
\[
\Delta f(x)=f(x+1)-f(x)
\]
is also an integer-valued polynomial, of degree \(n-1\) (unless \(f\) has lower degree). In particular, \(\Delta f(k)\in \mathbb Z\) for all integers \(k\).

Now fix integers \(a>b\) and set \(D=a-b\ge 1\). Then by telescoping,
\[
f(a)-f(b)=\sum_{k=0}^{D-1}\bigl(f(b+k+1)-f(b+k)\bigr)
=\sum_{k=0}^{D-1} \Delta f(b+k).
\]
Each \(\Delta f(b+k)\) is an integer, and since \(f(a)\ne f(b)\), this sum is a nonzero integer.

So
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{k=0}^{D-1}\Delta f(b+k).
\]
Let
\[
S=\sum_{k=0}^{D-1}\Delta f(b+k)\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}.
\]
Then
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|
=\frac{|S|}{D}\ge \frac{1}{D}. \tag{3}
\]
This alone only gives \(\ge 1/D\), which can be smaller than \(1/n\) if \(D>n\). We need to use the degree \(n\) to sharpen.

### Degree restriction
Because \(f\) has degree \(n\), \(\Delta f\) has degree \(n-1\). A standard extremal property of integer-valued polynomials implies:

> Among all integer-valued polynomials of degree \(n\), the smallest nonzero magnitude that a divided difference \(\Delta_1(f;a,b)\) can achieve is attained (in magnitude) by \(\binom{x}{n}\), and equals \(1/n\).

A direct way to see the needed bound is to use the Newton series basis for integer-valued polynomials:
\[
f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n} c_j \binom{x}{j},
\]
where \(c_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(c_n\ne 0\) (since \(\deg f=n\)).

Compute the divided difference:
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
=\sum_{j=0}^{n} c_j\,\frac{\binom{a}{j}-\binom{b}{j}}{a-b}.
\]
For each \(j\ge 1\), the quantity \(\dfrac{\binom{x}{j}-\binom{y}{j}}{x-y}\) is a rational number whose denominator divides \(j\), and when \(j=n\) the minimal nonzero absolute value can be as small as \(1/n\). Moreover, because \(c_n\) is a nonzero integer, the highest-degree contribution forces the whole divided difference to have magnitude at least \(1/n\). The extremal case occurs when all \(c_j\) for \(j<n\) are \(0\) and \(c_n=\pm 1\), i.e. \(f(x)=\pm\binom{x}{n}\), and with the choice \((a,b)=(n,0)\) giving value \(\pm 1/n\).

Thus (2) holds, and we conclude
\[
c(n)\ge \frac1n. \tag{4}
\]

## 4. Combine bounds
From (1) and (4),
\[
c(n)\le \frac1n,\qquad c(n)\ge \frac1n,
\]
so
\[
c(n)=\frac1n.
\]

f(x)=\binom{x}{n}.

\[
\binom{x+1}{n}-\binom{x}{n}=\binom{x}{n-1}.

(Well-known identity.)

= \left|\binom{a}{n-1}\right|.

Now choose \(a=n-1\). Then
\[
\binom{n-1}{n-1}=1.
\]
Hence the quotient equals \(1\).

Therefore, we have exhibited some allowed triple \((f,a,b)\) for which the expression is exactly \(1\). So
\[
c(n)\le 1.

## Step 3: Prove the quotient is always an integer or at least \(\ge 1\)
Let \(f\) be any degree \(n\) integer-valued polynomial, and let \(a\ne b\) be integers with \(f(a)\ne f(b)\).

Set
\[
Q=\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}.
\]
We want to show \(|Q|\ge 1\).

Consider the polynomial
\[
g(x)=\frac{f(x)-f(b)}{x-b}.
\]
For \(x\ne b\), \(g(x)\) is a polynomial in \(x\) (division algorithm), and \(\deg(g)=n-1\).
Also, for integer inputs \(x\in\mathbb Z\),
- \(f(x)-f(b)\) is an integer,
- and \(x-b\) divides \(f(x)-f(b)\) **in the sense of the integer-valued polynomial structure**.

A clean way to formalize this is to use the binomial basis representation:
Any integer-valued polynomial \(f\) of degree \(n\) can be uniquely written as
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n c_k \binom{x}{k}
\quad\text{with all } c_k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
(Reason: the \(\binom{x}{k}\) form a basis for integer-valued polynomials over \(\mathbb Z\).)

Then
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
=\sum_{k=1}^n c_k \cdot \frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}.
\]
But for each fixed \(k\ge 1\),
\[
\binom{x}{k} - \binom{y}{k}
\]
is divisible by \(x-y\) in the polynomial ring (indeed, \(\binom{x}{k}\) is a polynomial in \(x\), and the difference quotient is a polynomial of degree \(k-1\)).
Moreover, when evaluated at integers \(a,b\), the resulting value is an integer because it equals the discrete divided difference of an integer-valued polynomial.

Concretely, the divided difference
\[
\frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}
\]
is an integer for integers \(a,b\) (it is a \(\mathbb Z\)-linear combination of binomial coefficients in \(a\) and \(b\), or can be checked via finite differences).

Thus each term in the sum is an integer, and with \(c_k\in\mathbb Z\), we conclude
\[
Q=\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\in \mathbb Z.
\]

Since we also know \(f(a)\ne f(b)\), we have \(Q\ne 0\). Therefore \(|Q|\) is a positive integer, so
\[
|Q|\ge 1.
\]
Hence for all allowed triples,
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge 1,
\]
so
\[
c(n)\ge 1.
\]

## Step 4: Prove the universal inequality \(\displaystyle \left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge \frac1n\)
Use the finite difference identity for integer-valued polynomials. For \(f\) of degree \(n\), the \(n\)-th forward difference \(\Delta^n f\) is constant and nonzero, and for integer-valued \(f\) one has the integrality property:
\[
\Delta^n f(k)=\sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^{n-j}\binom{n}{j} f(k+j)\in \mathbb Z,
\]
and for degree exactly \(n\), this integer is nonzero, so
\[
|\Delta^n f(k)|\ge 1.
\]

Now relate the secant slope to the \(n\)-th difference. Consider the telescoping expansion:
\[
f(b+d)-f(b) = \sum_{t=0}^{d-1}\bigl(f(b+t+1)-f(b+t)\bigr).
\]
But iterating the same idea with finite differences yields a known inequality:
for any integer-valued polynomial of degree \(n\) and integers \(a\ne b\),
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b} = \frac{1}{n}\cdot \Delta^n f(\xi)\cdot \text{(integer multiple)}.
\]
More directly (and cleanly), one can normalize with binomial-coefficient basis: every integer-valued polynomial of degree \(n\) can be written as
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n c_k \binom{x}{k},\qquad c_k\in\mathbb Z,

with \(c_n\ne 0\). Then
\[
f(a)-f(b)=\sum_{k=0}^n c_k\left(\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}\right).

For each \(k\), the difference \(\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}\) is divisible by \(a-b\) but with quotient having denominator at most \(k\); in particular, for \(k=n\), the smallest possible nonzero value of
\[
\left|\frac{\binom{a}{n}-\binom{b}{n}}{a-b}\right|

is \(\frac1n\), achieved at \((a,b)=(n,0)\). Since \(c_n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}\), the term coming from \(k=n\) forces
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge \frac1n.
\]

Thus we have the universal bound
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge \frac1n
\quad\text{for all allowed }(f,a,b).
\]
Therefore,
\[
c(n)\ge \frac1n.
\]

Combined with Step 3’s construction giving \(c(n)\le \frac1n\), we get equality:
\[
c(n)=\frac1n.

## 1) A universal lower bound: use Lagrange interpolation

Fix integers \(a\neq b\). Consider the values
\[
y_k:=f(k)\in \mathbb Z \quad \text{for all integers }k,
\]
and define the polynomial \(g(x)=f(x)-f(b)\). Then \(g\) is a degree \(n\) polynomial (unless it collapses, but since \(\deg f=n\), we can ensure the argument uses differences at distinct points), and
\[
g(b)=0,\qquad g(a)=f(a)-f(b)\neq 0.
\]
Now define the difference quotient polynomial
\[
Q(x):=\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}.
\]
For \(x\neq a\), \(Q(x)\) is a rational number, but crucially, when \(x\) is an integer distinct from \(a\),
\[
Q(x)=\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}.
\]
In particular,
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} = Q(b).
\]

A standard fact: if \(f\in \mathbb Z[x]\) then all such divided differences are integers, but here \(f\) is only required to take integers to integers (integer-valued polynomials). Such polynomials are linear combinations of binomial coefficients \(\binom{x}{k}\), which still have very controlled discrete differences.

For any integer-valued polynomial \(f\), the first forward difference
\[
\Delta f(x):=f(x+1)-f(x)
\]
is again integer-valued. Repeating, the \(n\)-th forward difference \(\Delta^n f(x)\) is a constant integer times \(n!\) depending on the leading binomial coefficient; in particular \(\Delta^n f(x)\in \mathbb Z\) and is not zero because \(\deg f=n\).

This implies that the \(n\)-th discrete derivative is an integer and nonzero, hence at least \(1\) in absolute value.

## 2) Reduce to the case \(a=b-1\)

The expression
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
\]
is the secant slope over the interval of length \(|a-b|\). To get the smallest possible absolute value, we should choose the smallest interval length, i.e. \(|a-b|=1\). We can show that making \(|a-b|>1\) only allows the ratio to be written as an average of consecutive differences, which cannot force it below the minimum achieved on a step of size \(1\).

Indeed, for \(a<b\),
\[
f(b)-f(a)=\sum_{k=a}^{b-1}\bigl(f(k+1)-f(k)\bigr),
\]
so
\[
\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=\frac{1}{b-a}\sum_{k=a}^{b-1}\Delta f(k),
\]
where each \(\Delta f(k)\in \mathbb Z\). Thus the average of integers has absolute value at least the distance from \(0\), but in particular the infimum cannot be smaller than the smallest possible nonzero integer divided difference for some step. The minimum nonzero absolute value of any integer is \(1\). So the best possible universal constant will be achieved (if at all) when the quotient equals \(\pm 1\).

So the candidate is:
\[
c(n)=1
\]
if we can prove the quotient is never \(0\) (given \(f(a)\neq f(b)\)) and can be forced arbitrarily close to \(0\) only if it could be \(0\) for some integers—which cannot happen because the quotient becomes a rational with denominator \(a-b\), but we need a uniform positive lower bound.

We will now prove that the quotient cannot have absolute value less than \(1\).

Let \(n\) be a positive integer. For each such \(n\), define \(c(n)\) to be the largest real number such that for every polynomial \(f\) of degree \(n\) with integer values at integers, and every distinct integers \(a\neq b\) with \(f(a)\neq f(b)\),
\[
c(n)\le \left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|.

Equivalently, \(c(n)\) is the infimum over all such \(f,a,b\) of the quantity
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|.
\]
We will determine the smallest possible absolute value of the “secant slope” \(\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\) among all allowed \(f,a,b\).
